title: Generalized Abbreviation
statement:
You may shorten a string `word` by choosing some of its substrings (possibly none) and writing each chosen substring as its length in decimal. The chosen substrings must not overlap, and no two of them may touch: at least one kept letter has to separate any two of them. For example, `"abcde"` can become `"a3e"`, `"1bcd1"`, `"5"` or `"abcde"`, but not `"23"` or `"22de"` (the replaced pieces would be adjacent).

Return every abbreviation of `word` that can be made this way, each exactly once, in any order.
constraints: word contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Every letter is either kept or swallowed into a number, so there are exactly 2^n abbreviations, one per keep/replace choice for each letter. A maximal run of replaced letters becomes one number, which automatically keeps numbers apart. Backtracking walks this binary choice letter by letter, carrying how many letters are waiting to be written as a number. (A bitmask loop over all 2^n choices works too.)

## Approach

1. `backtrack(index, current, count)`: `current` is the text built so far and `count` is the number of replaced letters not yet written.
2. When `index` reaches the end, flush any pending `count` onto `current` and record it.
3. Branch 1, replace `word[index]`: recurse with `count + 1` and `current` unchanged.
4. Branch 2, keep `word[index]`: write the pending `count` (if any) as `prefix`, append the letter, and recurse with `count = 0`.
5. Start with `backtrack(0, '', 0)` and return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `"word"` the replace branch is tried first. Replacing all four letters reaches the end with `count = 4`, giving `"4"`. Backing up one level, `d` is kept after `count = 3`, so `prefix = "3"` and the result is `"3d"`. Next, with `count = 2` at `d`'s parent, `r` is kept (`"2r"`) and then `d` is replaced (`"2r1"`) or kept (`"2rd"`). Continuing this way produces the 16 strings from `"4"` to `"word"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · 2^n): there are 2^n results and building each string costs O(n).
- Space: O(n) recursion depth, plus the O(n · 2^n) output.

## Pitfalls

- Do not write a number for each replaced letter separately; consecutive replaced letters must merge (`"2"`, never `"11"`).
- Remember to flush a pending `count` at the end of the word, or results like `"wo2"` lose their tail.
- A count can reach two digits (up to 15), so append `count` as a number, not as a single character code.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `result` | every abbreviation found |
| `index` | position of the letter being decided |
| `current` | abbreviation text built so far |
| `count` | replaced letters waiting to be written as a number |
| `prefix` | `current` with the pending count written out |

narration.4: backtrack decides the letter at index, given the text so far and how many letters are waiting to become a number.
narration.6: Write any pending count and record the finished abbreviation.
narration.9: Choice 1: replace this letter, so the pending count grows by one.
narration.10: Choice 2 keeps the letter, so first write out the pending count, if any.
narration.11: Append the kept letter and continue with no pending count.
narration.14: Start at the first letter with empty text and nothing pending.
